Penny
pĕn´ĭ
n. (a day's wage; rendering Greek denarion)
The translators' rendering of the Roman denarius, using the familiar English coin. The denarius was a labourer's daily pay, which is the point in every parable that uses it.

Biblical Definition

A penny is the denarius, a day's wage. The householder agrees with labourers “for a penny a day” and pays the eleventh-hour men the same, provoking the complaint that shapes the parable (Mat 20:2,9–10). It is the coin brought to Christ in the tribute question: “Shew me the tribute money. And they brought unto him a penny” (Mat 22:19). Two hundred pennyworth of bread would not feed the multitude (Joh 6:7), and the good Samaritan leaves two pence with the innkeeper (Luk 10:35).

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828) defines penny as an ancient English silver coin; and notes it is used to denote the Roman denarius in the New Testament.

expand to see more

PENNY, n. An ancient English silver coin; but now an imaginary money of account, twelve of which are equal to a shilling.

2. Proverbially, a small sum.

3. Money in general.

Key Scripture

Mat 20:2 — "And when he had agreed with the labourers for a penny a day, he sent them into his vineyard."

Mat 20:9 — "And when they came that were hired about the eleventh hour, they received every man a penny."

Mat 22:19 — "Shew me the tribute money. And they brought unto him a penny."

Luk 10:35 — "And on the morrow when he departed, he took out two pence, and gave them to the host, and said unto him, Take care of him; and whatsoever thou spendest more, when I come again, I will repay thee."

Modern Corruption

The vineyard parable is heard as a lesson about fairness in wages, when its subject is grace — and the complaint it answers is the one respectable people always make about grace.

expand to see more

Matthew 20 is precise about the arithmetic so the offence lands. The first-hour men agreed for a penny; they received a penny; nothing was withheld. Their grievance is stated exactly: thou hast made them equal unto us, which have borne the burden and heat of the day. Nobody was cheated — someone else was treated generously, and that was intolerable. The householder's reply is the parable's hinge: is thine eye evil, because I am good?

The tribute penny in Matthew 22 turns on an image. Whose is this image and superscription? They say unto him, Caesar's. Then saith he unto them, Render therefore unto Caesar the things which are Caesar's; and unto God the things that are God's. The coin bore Caesar's image and went back to Caesar; the man asking bore God's image, and Christ leaves him to work out the implication.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Greek denarion (G1220), a Roman silver coin equal to a labourer's daily wage; dupsakion has no place here — the penny is always the denarius.

expand to see more

Greek denarion (G1220) — denarius, a day's wage; Matthew 20:2, 22:19, John 6:7, Revelation 6:6.

Greek assarion (G787) — farthing, a fraction of a denarius; Matthew 10:29, two sparrows sold for a farthing.

Greek lepton (G3016) — mite; Mark 12:42, the widow's two mites.

Usage

"“He agreed with the labourers for a penny a day” — nothing was withheld from anyone."

"“Is thine eye evil, because I am good?” — the parable's hinge."

"“Whose is this image and superscription?” — the coin, and the man holding it."
